extracted.intended_audience: Users/developers of Isabelle/Isar (Isabelle/HOL proof authors, proof engineers, interactive theorem prover users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing structured, human-readable Isar proofs and formal theory documents in the Isabelle/Isar framework (primarily for Isabelle/HOL). Covers proof style, language elements, block structure, induction, calculational reasoning, case-splitting, and document markup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-readable structured proofs (Isar goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isar stands for Intelligible semi-automated reasoning. The main purpose of the Isar language is to provide a conceptually different view on machine-checked proofs by offering a versatile environment for structured formal proof documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to write proofs as readable formal texts (drawing from informal mathematical prose and high-level programming languages). Writing human-readable proof texts requires additional effort by the writer, but properly written Isar proofs become accessible to a broader audience than unstructured tactic scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper language elements in final documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Isar commands may be either proper document constructors, or improper commands. Some proof methods and attributes are classified as improper; they are marked as improper and often helpful when developing proof documents, but their use is discouraged for the final human-readable outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagnostic commands and tactical-emulating commands only for experimentation or debugging. Remove or replace '∗' (improper) elements before presenting final proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use block-structured notepad semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal notepad is block structured. The fact produced by the last entry of a block is exported into the outer context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure proofs into explicit blocks or nested goal statements. Use 'next' to jump between sub-blocks. Understand that implicit blocks (e.g. nested 'have') introduce additional grouping that affects exported facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming conventions for identifiers and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower-case identifiers are usually preferred. Facts can be named after the main term within the proposition. Facts should not be named after the command that introduced them (assume, have). Natural numbers can be used as 'meaningless' names; symbolic identifiers are supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer descriptive names tied to the mathematical content, not the syntactic origin. Avoid misleading names like 'assume' or 'have' as fact names. Use simple numeric names where no semantic name is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing and referencing facts correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are simultaneous lists of theorems and can be produced via 'assume', 'have', 'note', 'let', etc. Facts can be referenced explicitly by name, implicitly via 'this', or by literal proposition notation (‹...›).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'assume a: A', 'have b: B', 'note c = a b'. Reference with 'note a', 'note this', or 'note ‹A›'. Instantiate facts with '[of ...]' or '[where ...]'. Use '[OF ...]' and '[THEN ...]' for backchaining/composition. Be careful with ad-hoc simplification (take care!).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project parts of multi-theorem facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Isar facts can contain multiple theorems; there is notation to project interval ranges or individual components of a fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use projections like 'note stuﬀ (1)', 'note stuﬀ (2−3)', 'note stuﬀ (2−)' to refer to specific components of a multi-theorem fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer calculational reasoning ('also' / 'finally')
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculational reasoning combines 'this' and a background 'calculation' fact using transitivity rules. Typical idiom: chain equalities/inequalities using 'also' and conclude with 'finally'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use library trans rules (e.g. 'trans', 'less_trans', 'less_le_trans') and the 'also' ... 'finally' pattern for readable equational/transitive chains. The '...' abbreviation can be used in intermediate steps. Ensure base types are suitable for mixed inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'moreover'/'ultimately' for degenerate calculations; prefer 'consider' for multi-branch
rubrics_metrics.description: Degenerate calculations append independent facts to the calculation (useful to avoid naming intermediates). 'moreover' / 'ultimately' collect such facts. For multi-branch case splitting, 'consider' (or 'cases') is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'have A', 'moreover have B', 'ultimately have A ∧ B' for aggregating independent facts. For branching (multiple exclusive cases), use 'consider' or 'cases' rather than degenerate calculation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction: prefer 'induct' method for structured proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'induct' proof method provides implicit rule selection and robust instantiation; it supplies context elements via symbolic case names and supports rule-structured induction statements with local parameters and premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'proof (induct n)' or 'proof (induct ... arbitrary: ...)' to get convenient, readable induction structure (case 0, case (Suc n), etc.). Avoid applying raw induction rules (e.g. 'proof (rule nat.induct)') which are fragile and lower-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid compact HOL formula anti-patterns in induction contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using compact HOL formulae with ∀ / −→ (i.e. heavy left-nesting of quantifiers/implications) is a well-known anti-pattern that produces useless formal noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write induction statements and hypotheses using explicit local parameters and premises rather than packing everything into compact ∀/−→ forms. Use 'induct' ability to pull out parameters/premises cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction with local parameters, premises and arbitrary instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The induct method can isolate local parameters and premises directly from the given statement; 'arbitrary:' is used to indicate variables that should be treated as arbitrary for the induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructs like 'proof (induct n arbitrary: x)' to get correct local contexts. Understand how arbitrary instances may be produced and used in subcases (e.g., access via ‹...›).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced induction over term subexpressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction over subexpressions of a certain shape can be handled by turning sub-expressions into a defined induction variable, often accompanied by fixing auxiliary parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define an induction variable for the sub-expression (e.g. 'assume A (a x) then have P (a x) proof (induct a x arbitrary: x)') and use the induction cases with their 'defn' and 'prem' facts to manage the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand theorems as natural deduction rule statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Isabelle/Pure theorems are natural deduction rules (premises => conclusion). Isar provides first-class notation for rule statements and the framework connectives '⇒' and '−→' indicate rule structure declaratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'print_statement' and 'thm' to inspect rule structure. Write and manipulate rule-style lemmas (introductions/eliminations) to align with Isar structured reasoning idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Isar context elements (fix / assume / define / obtain) correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Context elements introduce local constants, premises, definitions and obtained witnesses which are used to derive results; their semantics correspond to Pure connectives (e.g., fix → universal quantification, assume → implication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within blocks use 'fix x', 'assume A', 'define x where ...', 'obtain x where ...' and export the resulting facts properly. Remember that conclusions derived from an 'obtain' context may not mention the obtained variable afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid low-level Pure rule composition; prefer structured application
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure supports backward-chaining and rule composition via higher-order unification, but low-level rule composition is tedious and leads to unreadable / unmaintainable expressions in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer structured Isar idioms (fix/assume/show, 'then', 'proof (rule r)') and high-level methods rather than manually composing rules with '[OF]', '[THEN]' unless necessary for automation/debugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured backward reasoning: use fix / assume / show
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical proof decomposition is achieved via 'fix / assume / show', where the body produces a natural deduction rule to refine some goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write proofs top-down: open a 'proof −', 'fix ...', 'assume ...', 'show ...' and conclude with 'qed' to produce a readable structured derivation. Use implicit blocks where convenient but make the logical flow explicit for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured rule application pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose previous facts and new claims with a rule from the context/background by using patterns like 'then have C proof (rule r)' and supply remaining premises via nested sub-proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying a rule with multiple premises, provide some premises in an outer subproof (prefix of facts) and the remaining via inner 'show' sub-proof(s). For nested compound premises, use inner fix/assume/show blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized elimination and case-splitting: use 'cases', 'consider', and 'obtain'
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination rules typically have a prefix of assumptions and one or more cases. Isar provides native language elements, symbolic case names, and the 'cases' method to recover/elaborate this structure in a sub-proof. 'consider' states rules for generalized elimination/case splitting; 'obtain' inlines a single case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'proof (cases x rule: ...)', 'proof cases', or 'consider (a) A | (b) B | ...' followed by 'then ... proof cases' to structure multi-branch reasoning. Use 'obtain x where B x' to bring a single-case context into scope, remembering scope limits of the obtained variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use special names and background facts properly ('?thesis', 'this', '...','calculation')
rubrics_metrics.description: '?thesis' is the main conclusion of the innermost pending claim; 'this' refers to the last result produced in the text; '...' abbreviates the argument of the last explicitly stated result for infix application; calculational reasoning maintains a special fact called 'calculation' in the background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '?thesis' in case bodies to show the current goal, 'this' to refer to immediate prior facts, and '...' to shorten repeated RHS/LHS in calculational chains. Be aware of static vs dynamic behavior (e.g. '?thesis' is static inside some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer library-derived case rules and datatype 'cases' over manual splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Isabelle/HOL specification mechanisms (datatype, inductive, etc.) provide suitable derived cases rules that integrate naturally with 'cases' and 'obtain'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For datatype reasoning use 'proof (cases x)' and the automatically provided case names (e.g., 'case Foo', 'case (Bar a)') rather than inventing manual splitting patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs and formal content as theories/documents with markup
rubrics_metrics.description: Isabelle/Isar organizes definitions, statements and proofs as theories. A collection of theory sources may be presented as a printed document; document preparation uses markup commands, antiquotations and document markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the theory language and document markup (chapter 4 guidance) to produce readable, publishable theory documents; include appropriate 'text', 'section', 'title', 'author' and antiquotations to intermix formal and informal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readable structured Isar style over raw tactic scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Isar can assimilate old tactical style as an 'improper' sub-language (providing an upgrade path for existing tactic scripts), readable structured proofs are preferred as the primary proof format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high-level Isar constructs and methods ('simp', 'blast', 'induct', 'cases') and structure the narrative flow of proofs; only use tactical scripts/tactics for experimentation, proof search, or as last resort, and refactor them into structured Isar for presentation.
